title: Mexican Everyday Idioms
grammarNote: This lesson introduces no new tense; it focuses on high-frequency Mexican colloquialisms and verb+preposition idiomatic chunks used in casual, everyday speech. Register matters as much as meaning here — many of these expressions are warm and friendly among peers but out of place with elders, strangers, or in professional settings, so each phrase notes exactly where it fits.

phrases.vocabularyIntro: Very informal, used among friends and peers of similar age — avoid with elders, strangers, or in any business setting, where 'buenos días' or '¿cómo estás?' is expected.

exampleSentence.native: What's up, how has it been going?

phrases.grammarNote: 'Onda' literally means 'wave' or 'vibe'; '¿qué onda?' is fixed and doesn't conjugate like a normal question.
phrases.memoryHook: Think of catching someone's 'wave' or 'vibe' — '¿qué onda?' is asking what wave they're riding today.

phrases.vocabularyIntro: Informal, used to react with surprise among friends and family — it's a softened, non-vulgar alternative to a much stronger expression, but still avoid it with elders or in business settings.

exampleSentence.target: No manches, ¿en serio ganaste el premio?
exampleSentence.native: No way, seriously, did you win the prize?

phrases.grammarNote: 'Manches' comes from 'manchar' (to stain), but here it's purely idiomatic and has nothing to do with stains.
phrases.memoryHook: Picture someone dropping their jaw so hard it 'stains' the floor — that's the surprise behind 'no manches'.

practiceItems.prompt: ¿Cómo reaccionas si un amigo te da una noticia increíble?

phrases.native: Okay, see you in a bit
phrases.vocabularyIntro: 'Sale' as 'okay/deal' is informal and common among friends in Mexico; 'ahorita' (a diminutive of 'ahora') means 'in a little bit' — both are casual and unsuited for formal writing or business correspondence.

exampleSentence.target: Sale, nos vemos ahorita en tu casa.
exampleSentence.native: Okay, see you in a bit at your place.

phrases.grammarNote: 'Ahorita' can mean 'right now' or 'in a little while' depending on tone and context — a quirk unique to Mexican Spanish.
phrases.memoryHook: Think of 'sale' as closing a deal with a handshake — 'it's settled, see you ahorita'.

practiceItems.prompt: Translate: Okay, see you in a bit
¿A qué hora nos vemos, ahorita o más tarde?

phrases.native: I'm almost there, keep a lookout for me
phrases.vocabularyIntro: 'Ya merito' (almost there/almost time) and 'echar aguas' (to keep watch/give a heads-up) are both informal, everyday Mexican expressions used among friends — inappropriate in formal or professional contexts.

exampleSentence.target: Ya merito llego a la carne asada, échame aguas si llega mi jefe.
exampleSentence.native: I'm almost at the cookout, keep a lookout if my boss shows up.

phrases.grammarNote: 'Echar aguas' literally means 'to throw waters' but idiomatically means 'to watch out' or 'give a warning' — it doesn't relate to water at all.
phrases.memoryHook: Picture someone tossing water to warn others of danger ahead — that's the origin image behind 'echar aguas'.

practiceItems.prompt: Translate: I'm almost there, keep a lookout for me
¿Ya vas a llegar a la fiesta?

phrases.vocabularyIntro: 'Padrísimo' (super cool/awesome) is a friendly Mexican superlative built from 'padre' (cool) — informal and warm among friends, but too casual for formal writing.
'Ándale' (come on/hurry up/go ahead) is an all-purpose informal exclamation heard constantly in Mexico — casual among friends, not used in formal speech.

phrases.target: Me di cuenta de que ya es tarde
phrases.phonetic: meh dee KWEN-tah deh keh yah es TAR-deh

phrases.target: Quedamos de vernos a las ocho
phrases.native: We agreed to meet at eight
phrases.phonetic: keh-DAH-mos deh BEHR-nos ah lahs OH-cho

phrases.target: No me dejes dando el avión
phrases.native: Don't stand me up / leave me hanging
phrases.phonetic: no meh DEH-hes DAN-doh el ah-vee-ON

phrases.native: I'll call you in a bit

phrases.target: Ya me tengo que ir, al rato platicamos
phrases.native: I have to go now, we'll talk later
phrases.phonetic: yah meh TEN-goh keh eer, al RAH-toh plah-tee-KAH-mos

phrases.target: Está bien padre esta carne asada
phrases.phonetic: es-TAH bee-EN PAH-dreh ES-tah KAR-neh ah-SAH-dah

dialogue.scenario: Casual chat with friends at a carne asada get-together.

turns.speaker: npc
turns.native: What's up! You made it, awesome.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.cue: Greet them casually — ask what's up.

turns.speaker: npc
turns.line: Oye, ¿ya viste el carro nuevo de Beto? Se lo compró ayer.
turns.native: Hey, did you see Beto's new car? He bought it yesterday.

turns.speaker: npc
turns.line: Sí, está padrísimo. Bueno, ¿nos vemos otro rato para seguir platicando?
turns.native: Yeah, it's awesome. Okay, shall we meet up later to keep chatting?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.cue: Agree to meet up again in a bit.

turns.speaker: npc
turns.line: Va. Oye, ¿ya te vas? Apenas empezamos la carne asada.
turns.native: Deal. Hey, are you leaving already? We just started the cookout.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.cue: Say you have to go now, and you'll talk later.
